article:
**The quiet liability in AI image detection is the score**

The next fight over AI provenance may not be about whether a detector can spot a fake in a demo. It may be about who decided that a probabilistic score from a private model was good enough to remove evidence, flag a political ad, deny a claim, authenticate intelligence or accuse someone of deception.

That question has become more urgent because AI-content detection is moving from optional newsroom hygiene into compliance and security infrastructure. In the European Union, Article 50 transparency obligations under the AI Act began applying on August 2, 2026, including duties around marking, detecting and labelling artificially generated or manipulated content. NIST, in its synthetic-content transparency report, frames the field as a mix of provenance tracking, watermarking, detection, testing and auditing — not as a solved technical problem. ([ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-50))

A new NeurIPS 2026 paper by Kai Yao, submitted to arXiv on September 25, gives that policy shift a sharper technical edge. The paper studies “passive provenance”: trying to infer where an image came from by examining pixels alone, rather than reading a cryptographic credential or watermark. Its central warning is narrow but important: once a verifier exposes enough information through a public interface, an attacker may be able to learn a surrogate of the verifier and optimize images against it. In the paper’s controlled experiments, public CLIP-based verifiers failed under targeted pixel attacks on same-prompt real/diffusion benchmarks; the released code says all four evaluated source-target directions reached targeted attack success at an L∞ budget of 8/255 in one controlled public CLIP setting. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30997))

This is not proof that Hive, Sightengine, Reality Defender or any other commercial service can be defeated the same way. Yao’s repository is explicit about scope: it does not include datasets, image files, trained weights, query transcripts or experiment outputs, and it cautions that the finite-state experiment does not estimate the statistical limit for natural images. But the paper identifies the question that many buyers of AI verification tools are not asking publicly: what does the interface itself reveal? ([github.com](https://github.com/kaikaiyao/pixels-alone-provenance))

That matters because commercial image detectors often sell exactly what the paper treats as dangerous in public form: convenient confidence scores and source guesses.

Hive’s documentation says its AI-generated image and video detection API returns whether media is AI-generated, which model likely created it, and confidence scores for each classification. It lists source classes including Midjourney, DALL-E, Firefly, Stable Diffusion, Imagen, Sora, Grok and many others; it also says the confidence scores for each model head sum to one. Hive recommends customers consider the full API response because metadata can be stripped or falsified. ([docs.thehive.ai](https://docs.thehive.ai/docs/ai-image-and-video-detection))

Sightengine is even more explicit about the fallback logic. Its documentation says its AI image detector analyzes visual pixel content, does not use metadata, EXIF, C2PA provenance or invisible watermarks, and returns a confidence score from 0 to 1 that an image was produced or edited by a generative AI model. It markets use cases including moderation rules, bans on AI-generated imagery, misinformation control and fraud detection in fake IDs, profiles or claims. ([www-cf.sightengine.com](https://www-cf.sightengine.com/docs/ai-generated-image-detection))

Reality Defender’s published 1Kosmos technical datasheet shows how this moves from content moderation into identity systems. The document says Reality Defender is integrated into identity verification and authentication workflows, checks images and videos during onboarding and login, and returns a JSON response with status, score and model breakdown. It says all 1Kosmos identity-verification customers have Reality Defender deepfake detection in place, and claims deployment across enterprise verticals and Allied government customers. ([6858402.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na1.net](https://6858402.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na1.net/hubfs/6858402/DataSheets/Reality-Defender-Technical-Datasheet-4Dec2025.pdf))

Government adoption is already visible. The Defense Innovation Unit said on December 5, 2024, that Hive was one of the initial companies selected from 36 submissions to prototype deepfake detection and attribution technology for the Department of Defense. Hive said its initial two-year contract would support the intelligence community with offline, on-premise models for AI-generated video, image and audio content. ([diu.mil](https://www.diu.mil/latest/defense-innovation-unit-and-dod-collaborate-to-strengthen-synthetic-media))

The more defensible story, then, is not “AI detectors are useless.” Some work well in particular settings. NewsGuard’s May 2026 audit found Hive and Sightengine did not misidentify any of 15 authentic U.S.-Iran war-related photos as AI-generated in that test set. But the same audit found major disagreement among tools and weaker performance on significantly manipulated images: Sightengine identified five of 15 heavily altered images, while Hive identified nine of 15. NewsGuard also documented a case in which users cited a Hive result saying a video of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was likely AI-generated at 96.9 percent, although NewsGuard said contextual evidence confirmed the video’s authenticity. ([newsguardtech.com](https://www.newsguardtech.com/special-reports/leading-ai-image-detection-tools-mislead-online-users-often-declaring-authentic-content-fake/))

That is the accountability problem: a detector’s score can become a public allegation long before anyone understands what the score means.

Public agencies are starting to experience this. California’s Fair Political Practices Commission held an April 22, 2025, Public Outreach and Technology Committee panel on “Detecting AI in Campaign Advertisements,” with Hive CEO Kevin Guo and Adobe’s Andrew Kaback among the listed participants. The same agency’s complaint page now warns that its Enforcement Division has received complaints “generated and supported by incorrect AI analysis,” leading to rejection. The record does not say those complaints involved image detectors specifically, but it shows a regulator already managing bad AI-assisted evidentiary claims. ([fppc.ca.gov](https://www.fppc.ca.gov/events/public-outreach-and-technology/2025/april-22-2025-committee-agenda/?utm_source=openai))

There is an alternative model: active provenance. C2PA Content Credentials are designed as tamper-evident, cryptographically signed records that travel with media, and C2PA now describes a conformance program, trust list and certificate process for products that create credentials. OpenAI says images generated with ChatGPT, Codex or the OpenAI API include both Content Credentials and SynthID watermarks, while warning that metadata can be lost and that absence of a signal does not prove the content was not generated with OpenAI tools. Google DeepMind says SynthID embeds invisible watermarks into AI-generated media and is testing a SynthID Detector portal with journalists and media professionals. ([c2pa.org](https://c2pa.org/faqs/))

But active provenance has gaps: metadata can be stripped, watermarks can fail after heavy transformation, and unsigned media will remain common. That leaves pixel-only detectors as the fallback. The fallback is attractive because it is easy to integrate and returns a simple score. It is risky for the same reason.

The immediate accountability question is therefore not whether any single vendor is wrong. It is whether buyers — governments, platforms, insurers, banks, campaigns and newsrooms — are setting rules for how detector scores may be used, how thresholds are chosen, how errors are appealed, and how much interface information is exposed to users or adversaries.

Yao’s paper does not answer those procurement questions. It gives investigators and auditors a sharper one to ask: before an institution relies on a passive image verifier, has anyone tested not only its clean accuracy, but whether its public interface can be learned?
